newsitem.title: SPAIN: No obvious successor for Spain's Socialist leader.
newsitem.headline: No obvious successor for Spain's Socialist leader.

text.p: Spain's Socialist party leaders frantically cast about on Friday for the names of possible successors to former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez, who suddenly announced he would not run again for party chief.

Gonzalez, who took over the Socialist Workers' Party 24 years ago and led Spain for 13 of those years, unleashed an unprecedented power struggle at the 34th Congress of the party, where delegates have two days to elect a new leader.

"We have to be able in these two days to see which person will take the position of secretary-general. It's not going to be easy, because of Felipe's level of leadership and calibre in all aspects," said former Socialist social affairs minister Cristina Alberdi.
His successor will have the challenge of leading a credible opposition and rebuilding a demoralised party for the next general election, scheduled for the year 2000.
Party organisers said the executive committee would meet late on Friday to start discussing candidates and the shape of the next executive committee.
The leadership now has 36 members and there has been movement to reduce it to 20, with some or all of those positions up for election.

Regional party organisations were to present their nominations for secretary-general and the executive on Saturday with a final list of candidates expected to emerge late on Saturday or early on Sunday.
On Sunday, the final day of the congress, the entire body of delegates -- some 1,000 -- meet again and vote in their new leadership.
No clear front-runners emerged after Gonzalez's announcement on Friday. A list of the possible candidates mentioned most frequently follows, in alphabetical order:
-- Joaquin Almunia, Socialist party parliament president
-- Jose Bono, Castille La Mancha regional president
-- Cipria Ciscar, Socialist party organisation secretary
-- Alfredo Perez Rubalcaba, former Socialist government spokesman
-- Narcis Serra, former deputy prime minister

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, a former Spanish foreign minister, has also frequently been named as the best-qualified candidate, but party members said his current position was incompatible with the party leadership and he would probably not be interested.
"It could be Almunia, it could be another colleague, but I think there are many good candidates and many people who could take over under these circumstances," Alberdi said.
